summary: 47-page technical report for Kimi K3, a 2.8T-parameter (104B active) natively multimodal MoE with a 1M-token context built on Kimi Delta Attention, Attention Residuals and Stable LatentMoE. Covers architecture, pre-/post-training, agentic RL environments, infrastructure and an extensive evaluation (public benchmarks, in-house benchmarks, third-party leaderboards, cost efficiency). Its only safety evaluation is a dedicated two-tier cybersecurity capability section, corroborated by a joint UK AISI / US CAISI assessment; there is no evaluation of harmful-content refusal, jailbreaks, alignment or other misuse domains.

capability_benchmarks.name: PostTrainBench
capability_benchmarks.setting: Harbor, avg of 3 runs on H20

capability_benchmarks.name: BrowseComp
capability_benchmarks.setting: context compaction at 300K; 90.4 with full 1M no context management

evals: Tier 1: vulnerability discovery with PoC on real current codebases (OS kernels, databases, AI services, web frameworks, blockchain, VPN, internal infra)
Tier 2: in-house 36-task exploit-development suite (16 user-space real CVEs, 20 Linux kernel privilege-escalation tasks), GLM-5.2 baseline
UK AISI + US CAISI joint assessment (ExploitBench, 32-step simulated enterprise network)

metrics.name: Tier 1 human-confirmed rate of reviewed findings
metrics.value: ~70%; 16 previously unknown vulnerabilities across six projects

cyber.finding: Kimi K3 found real (including previously unknown) vulnerabilities and solved 38.9% of an expert-verified exploit suite, strongest on user-space targets; it struggles to complete exploit chains against hardened kernel targets. An independent AISI/CAISI assessment concurs it trails frontier cyber-capable models. Anthropic/OpenAI models were excluded because they refuse cyber tasks. No capability threshold, mitigation or deployment decision is tied to the results.
cyber.quote: Exploit development (Tier 2). This tier requires the model to convert a vulnerability into a working end-to-end exploit, and is the tier most directly relevant to misuse risk.

autonomy_ai_rnd.finding: AI-R&D-like and long-horizon autonomy benchmarks are reported only as capability results; no autonomy or self-improvement risk framing.

reward_hacking.finding: Reward-hacking attempts and unintended destructive agent operations are cited as motivation for the isolated AgentENV microVM sandbox; no measurement of reward hacking is reported.
reward_hacking.quote: As agents become more capable and tasks more difficult, they tend to explore more aggressively and may even attempt reward hacking.

evals: in-house Faithfulness benchmark (fact-checker verified hallucination rate)
honesty_hallucination.finding: Single in-house hallucination metric reported within 'conversational experience'; K3 is near the top of the comparison set.
honesty_hallucination.quote: Faithfulness: measures factual hallucination rates in model responses, with each response verified by a fact checker.

evals: AgentENV Firecracker microVM isolation for RL/eval
system_safeguards.finding: Only training/eval sandbox isolation is described (after kernel panics and deadlocks from unintended agent operations in container sandboxes); no deployment safeguards, classifiers or misuse mitigations for the released open weights.
system_safeguards.quote: in our early experiments with traditional container-based sandbox runtimes, we observed several kernel panics and deadlocks caused by unintended agent operations.

notable_new_eval_methods: Two-tier cybersecurity evaluation (vulnerability discovery on live codebases + 36-task expert-verified exploit suite, ~540 expert-hours) — first cyber section in a Kimi report (p.30-31)
In-house agent suites: 24/7 ClawBench 2.0, MIRA Bench, KAET, CLIF Bench, Agentic Vision Bench, Swarm Bench, Agent Behavior Bench (process quality/discipline), Faithfulness (p.28-30)
AgentENV microVM sandbox for agentic RL (p.22)

self_reported_limitations.text: We regard our evaluation as a lower bound on capability. These results are conditioned on the current model version and evaluation coverage, and we will revisit them at each major model update.
Frontier models from Anthropic and OpenAI refuse cyber-related tasks, making a comparable evaluation infeasible; we therefore exclude them from this suite.
For WorldVQA, we observe consistent refusal behavior across models and enforce an answer via prompt engineering.
The results of Claude Fable 5 include fallback behaviors and the results of GPT-5.6 Sol include potential cyberguards.
research-level reasoning remains a key direction for improvement.

notes: KEY: first Kimi document with any dedicated safety-relevant evaluation, and it is cyber-only, framed as capability measurement ('increasing operational risk', 'misuse risk') with a third-party government (AISI/CAISI) assessment cited. No framework, thresholds, or mitigations; no harmful-content, jailbreak, CBRN, alignment, sycophancy, bias or child-safety evaluation. Refusals are discussed only for competitor models (Claude Fable 5 refusals/fallbacks in in-house benchmarks, Anthropic/OpenAI refusing cyber tasks) and to force answers on WorldVQA — treated as an obstacle to measurement rather than a safety property. Agent Behavior Bench scores 'tool-use behavior, efficiency, and discipline' (process quality, not safety).
